name: P2 · Unit 1 — Fundamentals of Computers (complete)
description: All 7 topics of Unit 1 split into 20 syllabus sub-topics, 30 questions each: introduction, functional units, evolution, generations, classification, applications, I/O and memory devices, software, problem solving, Word, Excel, PowerPoint, configuration, motherboard, memory, power supply, assembling.

questions.question: A computer is best defined as an electronic device that:

options.A: Accepts data, processes it under the control of stored instructions, and produces and stores results
options.C: Works only when connected to the Internet
options.D: Thinks and takes decisions on its own

questions.subject: Introduction to Computers
questions.explanation: A computer accepts input, processes it according to a stored program, produces output and can store data and results.

questions.question: The characteristic 'diligence' of a computer means that it:

options.D: Works for long hours without fatigue or loss of accuracy

questions.subject: Introduction to Computers
questions.explanation: Unlike humans, a computer does not get tired or lose concentration while performing repetitive work.

questions.question: GIGO in computing stands for:
questions.subject: Introduction to Computers
questions.explanation: If the input data or instructions are wrong, the output will also be wrong, even if the computer works perfectly.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of a computer?

options.A: Ability to take independent decisions without instructions

questions.subject: Introduction to Computers
questions.explanation: Computers have no intelligence of their own (zero IQ); they only follow instructions.

questions.question: 'Information' differs from 'data' because information is:

options.B: Processed data that is meaningful and useful for decision making

questions.subject: Introduction to Computers
questions.explanation: Data are raw facts; processing turns them into information such as totals, averages and reports.

questions.question: According to P. K. Sinha, the five basic operations performed by every computer are:

options.A: Inputting, storing, processing, outputting and controlling
options.B: Compiling, linking, loading, executing and debugging
options.C: Typing, printing, scanning, copying and saving
options.D: Fetching, decoding, executing, storing and printing

questions.subject: Introduction to Computers
questions.explanation: These five operations are carried out by the input, storage, processing (CPU), output and control units.

questions.question: One nanosecond equals:
questions.subject: Introduction to Computers

questions.question: Arrange the time units from the longest to the shortest:
questions.subject: Introduction to Computers
questions.explanation: Each step down is a factor of 1000: ms (10^-3), µs (10^-6), ns (10^-9), ps (10^-12).

questions.question: 'Versatility' as a characteristic of computers means:

options.A: They can perform a wide variety of tasks

questions.subject: Introduction to Computers
questions.explanation: The same computer can be used for word processing, calculations, games, communication and much more.

questions.question: In computing, the term 'liveware' (humanware) refers to:

options.B: The people who operate and use computers

questions.subject: Introduction to Computers
questions.explanation: A computer system consists of hardware, software and liveware (users, operators, programmers).

questions.question: The 'word length' of a computer is:

options.A: The number of words stored in RAM
options.B: The number of bits the CPU processes as a single unit
options.C: The number of characters in a word document

questions.subject: Introduction to Computers
questions.explanation: A 64-bit processor handles 64-bit words in its registers and ALU operations.

questions.question: MIPS, used as a measure of processor performance, stands for:
questions.subject: Introduction to Computers
questions.explanation: MIPS counts how many millions of instructions a processor executes per second.

questions.question: A processor clock of 3 GHz produces how many clock cycles per second?
questions.subject: Introduction to Computers
questions.explanation: Giga = 10^9, so 3 GHz = 3 × 10^9 cycles per second.

questions.question: The smallest unit of data in a computer is the:
questions.subject: Introduction to Computers
questions.explanation: A bit (binary digit) is 0 or 1; 4 bits make a nibble and 8 bits make a byte.

questions.question: In binary units, 1 TB is equal to:
questions.subject: Introduction to Computers
questions.explanation: 1 KB = 1024 bytes, 1 MB = 1024 KB, 1 GB = 1024 MB and 1 TB = 1024 GB.

questions.question: Which of the following is information rather than raw data?

options.A: A class report card showing each student's total and rank
options.B: The marks 45, 67 and 89 written on a paper
options.C: The digits typed at a keyboard

questions.subject: Introduction to Computers
questions.explanation: Totals and ranks are the result of processing raw marks, so they are information.

questions.question: A computer's ability to carry out a whole program without human intervention once started is called:
questions.subject: Introduction to Computers
questions.explanation: The stored program lets the computer perform all the steps automatically.

questions.question: Digital computers operate on:
questions.subject: Introduction to Computers
questions.explanation: Digital computers represent all data as discrete binary digits.

questions.question: Which statement about computers is correct?

options.A: A computer has no common sense and follows instructions exactly as given
options.B: A computer can correct wrong instructions by itself
options.C: A computer feels tired after long work
options.D: A computer learns only from emotions

questions.subject: Introduction to Computers
questions.explanation: A computer cannot judge whether instructions are sensible; it just executes them.

questions.question: The data processing cycle is correctly represented as:
questions.subject: Introduction to Computers
questions.explanation: Data are input, processed, and the results are output and/or stored (the IPO cycle).

questions.question: Which of the following is liveware in a computer system?
questions.subject: Introduction to Computers
questions.explanation: People such as programmers and operators form the liveware.

questions.question: A computer with a 2 GHz clock completes one clock cycle in:
questions.subject: Introduction to Computers
questions.explanation: Cycle time = 1 / frequency = 1 / (2 × 10^9) s = 0.5 × 10^-9 s = 0.5 ns.

questions.question: Most errors in computer output are caused by:

options.C: Human errors in input data or programs

questions.subject: Introduction to Computers
questions.explanation: Modern hardware is extremely reliable; errors usually come from incorrect data or program logic (GIGO).

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. A computer can take decisions without being given any program.
II. A computer never needs input data to produce useful output.
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: Introduction to Computers
questions.explanation: Both are false: a computer follows programs and needs input data to process.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): A computer can produce wrong results even when its hardware works perfectly.
Reason (R): Computers can work continuously for long hours without fatigue.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Introduction to Computers
questions.explanation: Both statements are true, but diligence does not explain wrong results; the real reason is GIGO (wrong input or program).

questions.question: Hardware refers to:

options.A: The programs that run on a computer
options.C: The physical, tangible components of a computer

questions.subject: Introduction to Computers
questions.explanation: Keyboards, CPUs, memory chips and monitors are hardware; programs are software.

questions.question: How many bytes are there in 1 KB (binary)?
questions.subject: Introduction to Computers

questions.question: Which unit is used to measure the storage capacity of memory?
questions.subject: Introduction to Computers
questions.explanation: Storage is measured in bytes (KB, MB, GB, TB); hertz measures frequency.

questions.question: The term 'computer' is derived from the word 'compute', which means:
questions.subject: Introduction to Computers
questions.explanation: Early computers were built mainly to perform calculations.

questions.question: Which of the following is a limitation of computers?

options.A: Lack of feelings, judgement and common sense

questions.subject: Introduction to Computers
questions.explanation: Computers cannot use judgement or feelings; the other options are strengths.

sets.name: 2 · Functional Components & Working of Each Unit

questions.question: Which unit of a computer converts data entered by the user into binary form that the computer can understand?
questions.subject: Functional Components & Working of Each Unit
questions.explanation: Input devices capture data and convert them into machine-readable binary codes.

questions.question: The Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU) performs:

options.B: Arithmetic operations and logical operations such as comparisons

questions.subject: Functional Components & Working of Each Unit
questions.explanation: The ALU adds, subtracts, compares values (>, <, =) and performs logical AND, OR and NOT.

questions.question: Which of the following operations is performed by the ALU?

options.A: Comparing two numbers to see which is larger

questions.subject: Functional Components & Working of Each Unit
questions.explanation: Comparisons are logical operations carried out by the ALU; fetching and decoding are control-unit tasks.

questions.question: The Control Unit is often compared to the human:

options.B: Central nervous system, which coordinates all activities

questions.subject: Functional Components & Working of Each Unit
questions.explanation: The CU directs and coordinates the other units, just as the nervous system coordinates the body.

questions.question: The Central Processing Unit consists of:
questions.subject: Functional Components & Working of Each Unit
questions.explanation: The CPU contains the ALU, the control unit and a set of fast registers.

questions.question: Which register usually stores the result of an arithmetic or logic operation?
questions.subject: Functional Components & Working of Each Unit
questions.explanation: In accumulator-based architectures, the accumulator holds one operand and the result of ALU operations.

questions.question: The Memory Address Register (MAR) holds:

options.D: The address of the memory location to be read or written

questions.subject: Functional Components & Working of Each Unit
questions.explanation: The MAR sends the address to memory over the address bus.

questions.question: The Memory Data Register (MDR/MBR) holds:

options.C: The data being transferred to or from memory
options.D: The address of the next instruction

questions.subject: Functional Components & Working of Each Unit
questions.explanation: Data read from memory, or to be written to memory, pass through the MDR.

questions.question: The Instruction Register (IR) contains:

options.C: The result of the last addition
options.D: The instruction currently being decoded and executed

questions.subject: Functional Components & Working of Each Unit
questions.explanation: After fetching, the instruction is placed in the IR so the control unit can decode it.

questions.question: The address bus is:

options.C: Unidirectional, carrying addresses from the CPU to memory and I/O

questions.subject: Functional Components & Working of Each Unit
questions.explanation: Only the CPU places addresses on the address bus.

questions.question: The data bus is:

options.A: Unidirectional from memory to CPU only
options.B: Bidirectional, carrying data to and from the CPU

questions.subject: Functional Components & Working of Each Unit
questions.explanation: Data move both ways: from memory to the CPU when reading and from the CPU to memory when writing.

questions.question: The control bus carries:

options.B: Signals such as memory read/write, interrupt requests and clock

questions.subject: Functional Components & Working of Each Unit
questions.explanation: Control signals coordinate the timing and direction of transfers.

questions.question: A CPU with 16 address lines can address how many memory locations?
questions.subject: Functional Components & Working of Each Unit

questions.question: The basic instruction cycle consists of:
questions.subject: Functional Components & Working of Each Unit
questions.explanation: The CPU fetches an instruction, decodes it and executes it, then repeats.

questions.question: Which part of the CPU decodes the opcode of an instruction?
questions.subject: Functional Components & Working of Each Unit
questions.explanation: The control unit interprets the opcode and issues control signals.

questions.question: Secondary storage differs from primary memory because it is:

options.A: Non-volatile, larger and slower, and not directly accessed by the CPU

questions.subject: Functional Components & Working of Each Unit
questions.explanation: Hard disks and SSDs keep data without power but must be loaded into RAM before processing.

questions.question: The output unit:

options.A: Converts binary results into a form understandable by humans

questions.subject: Functional Components & Working of Each Unit
questions.explanation: Monitors, printers and speakers present results in human-readable form.

questions.question: Main memory is also called:
questions.subject: Functional Components & Working of Each Unit
questions.explanation: RAM is the primary (main) memory directly accessible by the CPU.

questions.question: Which component sets the pace at which the CPU performs its operations?
questions.subject: Functional Components & Working of Each Unit
questions.explanation: The clock generates regular pulses that synchronise CPU operations.

questions.question: Which of the following is the fastest storage in a computer?
questions.subject: Functional Components & Working of Each Unit
questions.explanation: Registers are inside the CPU and are accessed within a single clock cycle.

questions.question: The flag (status) register records:

options.B: The address of the next instruction
options.D: Conditions such as zero, carry, sign and overflow after an operation

questions.subject: Functional Components & Working of Each Unit
questions.explanation: Branch instructions test these flags to take decisions.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a function of the control unit?

options.B: Performing the addition of two numbers

questions.subject: Functional Components & Working of Each Unit
questions.explanation: Addition is done by the ALU.

questions.question: After an instruction is fetched, the program counter is:

options.D: Incremented to point to the next instruction

questions.subject: Functional Components & Working of Each Unit
questions.explanation: The PC is incremented (unless a jump changes it) so the next instruction can be fetched.

questions.question: The width of the data bus mainly determines:

options.D: How much data can be transferred at one time

questions.subject: Functional Components & Working of Each Unit
questions.explanation: A 64-bit data bus moves 64 bits per transfer; the address bus width determines the memory size.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. The width of the address bus determines the maximum memory that can be addressed.
II. The width of the data bus determines the maximum memory that can be addressed.
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: Functional Components & Working of Each Unit
questions.explanation: n address lines give 2^n addressable locations; the data bus affects transfer size, not memory size.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): The control unit is called the nerve centre of the computer.
Reason (R): It directs and coordinates the operations of all the other units.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Functional Components & Working of Each Unit
questions.explanation: Coordinating all units is exactly why it is called the nerve centre.

questions.question: How many bytes does a 32-bit data bus transfer in one bus cycle?
questions.subject: Functional Components & Working of Each Unit
questions.explanation: 32 bits ÷ 8 = 4 bytes.

questions.question: In a stored-program (von Neumann) computer, instructions and data are held in:
questions.subject: Functional Components & Working of Each Unit
questions.explanation: Both share one memory, which is the essence of the stored-program concept.

questions.question: General-purpose registers are used to:

options.C: Temporarily hold data and intermediate results during processing

questions.subject: Functional Components & Working of Each Unit
questions.explanation: They are fast working storage for the CPU.

questions.question: Which unit stores data and instructions before, during and after processing?
questions.subject: Functional Components & Working of Each Unit
questions.explanation: The memory unit holds programs, data and results.

questions.question: Which is considered the earliest known calculating device?
questions.subject: Evolution of Computers
questions.explanation: The abacus, using beads on rods, was used thousands of years ago in Mesopotamia and China.

questions.question: Napier's bones (1617), used for multiplication, were invented by:
questions.subject: Evolution of Computers
questions.explanation: John Napier, the Scottish mathematician who also introduced logarithms.

questions.question: The slide rule, based on logarithms, was invented by:
questions.subject: Evolution of Computers
questions.explanation: William Oughtred developed the slide rule around 1620–1630.

questions.question: The Pascaline (1642), a mechanical calculator, could perform:

options.B: All four arithmetic operations and square roots

questions.subject: Evolution of Computers
questions.explanation: Blaise Pascal's machine added and subtracted using gears; Leibniz's Stepped Reckoner could also multiply and divide.

questions.question: The Stepped Reckoner, which could also multiply and divide, was built by:
questions.subject: Evolution of Computers
questions.explanation: Leibniz improved on Pascal's design with his stepped drum mechanism.

questions.question: Joseph Marie Jacquard's loom (1804) is important in computing history because it used:

options.D: Punched cards to control the weaving pattern

questions.subject: Evolution of Computers
questions.explanation: The idea of storing instructions on punched cards later influenced Babbage and Hollerith.

questions.question: Charles Babbage is called the 'father of the computer' mainly because of his design of the:
questions.subject: Evolution of Computers
questions.explanation: The Analytical Engine (1830s) had a store, a mill, control via punched cards and output, like a modern computer.

questions.question: Babbage's Difference Engine was designed to:

options.A: Calculate polynomial tables using the method of finite differences

questions.subject: Evolution of Computers
questions.explanation: It was meant to compute mathematical tables automatically and accurately.

questions.question: Who is regarded as the world's first computer programmer?
questions.subject: Evolution of Computers
questions.explanation: Ada Lovelace wrote an algorithm for the Analytical Engine to compute Bernoulli numbers.

questions.question: Herman Hollerith's tabulating machine was first used for the:
questions.subject: Evolution of Computers
questions.explanation: It processed punched cards and greatly reduced the time needed to tabulate the census.

questions.question: The company founded by Herman Hollerith later became:
questions.subject: Evolution of Computers
questions.explanation: The Tabulating Machine Company merged into CTR, renamed IBM in 1924.

questions.question: The Harvard Mark I (1944), designed by Howard Aiken with IBM, was:
questions.subject: Evolution of Computers
questions.explanation: Mark I used electromechanical switches and relays and read instructions from punched paper tape.

questions.question: The Atanasoff–Berry Computer (ABC) is significant as:

options.D: One of the first electronic digital computers, using vacuum tubes and binary arithmetic

questions.subject: Evolution of Computers
questions.explanation: John Atanasoff and Clifford Berry built it at Iowa State between 1937 and 1942.

questions.question: ENIAC was developed by:

options.B: Alan Turing and John von Neumann
options.D: J. Presper Eckert and John Mauchly

questions.subject: Evolution of Computers
questions.explanation: ENIAC was built at the University of Pennsylvania and completed in 1945–46.

questions.question: ENIAC was programmed by:

options.B: Loading programs from a hard disk

questions.subject: Evolution of Computers
questions.explanation: ENIAC was not a stored-program computer at first; reprogramming meant rewiring.

questions.question: The 'First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC' (1945), which described the stored-program concept, was written by:
questions.subject: Evolution of Computers
questions.explanation: This report gave its name to the von Neumann architecture.

questions.question: EDSAC (1949), one of the first practical stored-program computers, was built at:
questions.subject: Evolution of Computers
questions.explanation: EDSAC ran its first program in May 1949.

questions.question: Colossus (1943–44), used for breaking German codes, was built in:

options.A: Britain, at Bletchley Park, by Tommy Flowers

questions.subject: Evolution of Computers
questions.explanation: Colossus was an electronic, programmable machine used for code-breaking.

questions.question: Konrad Zuse's Z3 (1941) was:

options.A: The first programmable, fully automatic electromechanical computer

questions.subject: Evolution of Computers
questions.explanation: The Z3 used relays and binary floating-point arithmetic.

questions.question: In 1936 Alan Turing described an abstract model of computation now known as the:
questions.subject: Evolution of Computers
questions.explanation: The Turing machine defines what can be computed algorithmically.

questions.question: The first computer installed in India (1956) was the HEC-2M at the:
questions.subject: Evolution of Computers
questions.explanation: The ISI, founded by P. C. Mahalanobis, installed the HEC-2M in 1956.

questions.question: TIFRAC, the first computer designed and built in India, was developed at:

options.D: Tata Institute of Fundamental Research (TIFR), Mumbai

questions.subject: Evolution of Computers
questions.explanation: TIFRAC (TIFR Automatic Calculator) was commissioned in 1960.

questions.question: Arrange chronologically: ENIAC, Analytical Engine design, Pascaline, UNIVAC I.

options.A: ENIAC → Pascaline → UNIVAC I → Analytical Engine
options.B: Analytical Engine → Pascaline → UNIVAC I → ENIAC
options.C: Pascaline → Analytical Engine → ENIAC → UNIVAC I
options.D: Pascaline → ENIAC → Analytical Engine → UNIVAC I

questions.subject: Evolution of Computers
questions.explanation: 1642, 1830s, 1945–46 and 1951 respectively.

questions.question: UNIVAC I became famous in 1952 for:

options.A: Correctly predicting the result of the US presidential election

questions.subject: Evolution of Computers
questions.explanation: On live TV, UNIVAC predicted Eisenhower's landslide victory.

questions.question: Which of the following machines was electromechanical rather than fully electronic?
questions.subject: Evolution of Computers
questions.explanation: Mark I used relays; the others used vacuum tubes.

questions.question: In Babbage's Analytical Engine, the 'Store' corresponds to:
questions.subject: Evolution of Computers
questions.explanation: The Store held numbers; the Mill performed calculations.

questions.question: ECIL (Electronics Corporation of India Ltd), which manufactured some of India's early indigenous computers, is headquartered in:
questions.subject: Evolution of Computers
questions.explanation: ECIL, set up under the Department of Atomic Energy in 1967, is based in Hyderabad.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. The Analytical Engine was fully built and used during Babbage's lifetime.
II. Ada Lovelace wrote an algorithm intended for the Analytical Engine.
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: Evolution of Computers
questions.explanation: The Analytical Engine was never completed in Babbage's lifetime; Lovelace's notes (1843) contain an algorithm for computing Bernoulli numbers.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Punched cards played an important role in early data processing.
Reason (R): Charles Babbage introduced punched cards for processing the 1890 US census.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Evolution of Computers
questions.explanation: A is true. R is false: Herman Hollerith used punched cards for the 1890 census (Jacquard had used them for looms in 1804).

questions.question: The stored-program concept was first put into practice in the late 1940s by machines such as:
questions.subject: Evolution of Computers
questions.explanation: The Manchester Baby (1948) and EDSAC (1949) stored their programs in memory.

questions.question: First-generation computers (about 1940–1956) used:
questions.subject: Generations of Computers
questions.explanation: Vacuum tubes were large, hot and unreliable.

questions.question: Second-generation computers (about 1956–1963) were based on:
questions.subject: Generations of Computers
questions.explanation: Transistors were smaller, faster, cheaper and more reliable than tubes.

questions.question: Third-generation computers (about 1964–1971) were based on:
questions.subject: Generations of Computers
questions.explanation: ICs placed many transistors on a single chip.

questions.question: Fourth-generation computers (1971 onwards) are characterised by:
questions.subject: Generations of Computers
questions.explanation: An entire CPU was put on a single chip (e.g. Intel 4004).

questions.question: Fifth-generation computing is mainly associated with:

options.B: Artificial intelligence, parallel processing and ULSI

questions.subject: Generations of Computers
questions.explanation: Japan's Fifth Generation Computer Systems project (1982) focused on AI and parallel processing.

questions.question: First-generation computers were programmed mainly in:
questions.subject: Generations of Computers
questions.explanation: Programs were written in binary machine code; assembly came into wide use in the second generation.

questions.question: High-level languages such as FORTRAN and COBOL came into use during the:
questions.subject: Generations of Computers
questions.explanation: FORTRAN (1957) and COBOL (1959) appeared with transistorised computers.

questions.question: Magnetic core memory was the main primary memory of:
questions.subject: Generations of Computers
questions.explanation: Second-generation machines used magnetic cores; first-generation machines often used magnetic drums.

questions.question: Which of the following was a second-generation computer?
questions.subject: Generations of Computers
questions.explanation: The IBM 1401 (1959) used transistors; the System/360 (1964) used ICs.

questions.question: The IBM System/360 (1964) belongs to the:
questions.subject: Generations of Computers
questions.explanation: It was one of the most famous third-generation families using IC-based technology.

questions.question: Operating systems with multiprogramming became common in the:
questions.subject: Generations of Computers
questions.explanation: Third-generation computers had operating systems allowing several programs in memory.

questions.question: The transistor was invented in 1947 at:
questions.subject: Generations of Computers
questions.explanation: Bardeen, Brattain and Shockley invented it at Bell Labs.

questions.question: The integrated circuit was invented independently by:
questions.subject: Generations of Computers
questions.explanation: Kilby (Texas Instruments, 1958) and Noyce (Fairchild, 1959).

questions.question: The first commercial microprocessor, the Intel 4004, was released in:
questions.subject: Generations of Computers
questions.explanation: The 4004 marked the beginning of the fourth generation.

questions.question: The IBM Personal Computer was launched in:
questions.subject: Generations of Computers
questions.explanation: The IBM PC (1981) used the Intel 8088 processor and MS-DOS.

questions.question: Which generation had the problems of high heat, huge size and frequent breakdowns?
questions.subject: Generations of Computers
questions.explanation: Thousands of vacuum tubes produced great heat and often burned out.

questions.question: Keyboards and monitors replaced punched cards and printouts as the main interface in the:
questions.subject: Generations of Computers
questions.explanation: Third-generation systems introduced interactive use through keyboards and monitors.

questions.question: Graphical user interfaces, personal computers and networking became widespread in the:
questions.subject: Generations of Computers
questions.explanation: GUIs, PCs and the Internet belong to the microprocessor era.

questions.question: Which technology term refers to integrating a very large number of transistors (thousands to millions) on one chip?
questions.subject: Generations of Computers
questions.explanation: SSI, MSI, LSI, VLSI and ULSI indicate increasing levels of integration.

questions.question: Arrange the generations' main electronic components in order:
questions.subject: Generations of Computers
questions.explanation: This is the standard classification of the first four generations.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a first-generation computer?
questions.subject: Generations of Computers
questions.explanation: UNIVAC I used vacuum tubes.

questions.question: The PDP-8 (1965), a popular minicomputer, belongs to the:
questions.subject: Generations of Computers
questions.explanation: Minicomputers like the PDP-8 were made possible by IC technology.

questions.question: Which statement about fourth-generation computers is correct?

options.B: Their entire CPU could be placed on a single chip

questions.subject: Generations of Computers
questions.explanation: The microprocessor made small, affordable personal computers possible.

questions.question: The Apple II (1977) belongs to which generation?
questions.subject: Generations of Computers
questions.explanation: It was an early microprocessor-based personal computer.

questions.question: Which input/output media were typical of first-generation computers?
questions.subject: Generations of Computers
questions.explanation: Input was via punched cards and output via printouts.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. Transistor-based computers consumed less power than vacuum-tube computers.
II. Third-generation computers used integrated circuits.
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: Generations of Computers
questions.explanation: Both are correct.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Fourth-generation computers are much cheaper and smaller than earlier ones.
Reason (R): VLSI technology places a whole processor on a single chip.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Generations of Computers
questions.explanation: Mass-produced microprocessors reduced size and cost dramatically.

questions.question: Natural language processing, expert systems and robotics are goals typically associated with:
questions.subject: Generations of Computers
questions.explanation: These AI goals characterise fifth-generation computing.

questions.question: In which generation did time-sharing and remote terminals become common?
questions.subject: Generations of Computers
questions.explanation: Time-sharing systems allowed many users to share a computer interactively.

questions.question: Which device made second-generation computers more reliable than first-generation ones?
questions.subject: Generations of Computers
questions.explanation: Transistors had no filament to burn out and produced much less heat.

questions.question: On the basis of working principle, computers are classified as:
questions.subject: Classification of Computers
questions.explanation: Analog computers use continuous quantities, digital computers discrete values, and hybrids combine both.

questions.question: An analog computer works on:

options.C: Continuously varying physical quantities such as voltage, temperature or pressure

questions.subject: Classification of Computers
questions.explanation: Examples include speedometers and older analog simulators.

questions.question: Which of these is an example of an analog device?
questions.subject: Classification of Computers
questions.explanation: A thermometer shows a continuously varying quantity.

questions.question: On the basis of size and capacity, computers are classified as:
questions.subject: Classification of Computers
